newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Top N.Korean officers climb hierarchy - Seoul.
newsitem.headline: Top N.Korean officers climb hierarchy - Seoul.

text.p: A North Korean marshal and two vice-marshals have been listed in the top seven of the Stalinist country's ruling hierarchy in a political shift towards the military, analysts said on Monday.
"It is unprecedented that three military figures have been listed in such high positions," said Park Sung-hoon, a director general at the Unification Ministry in Seoul.
Park said the three officers were listed among the seven top leaders when Pyongyang released its hierarchy during a military parade on Friday.
The parade marked the 65th anniversary of the army.
"(North Korean leader) Kim Jong-il depends almost solely on the military to maintain the country's system," Park said.
Marshal Ri Ul-sol and vice marshals Jo Myong-rok and Kim Yong-chun were ranked only behind Kim Jong-il, supreme commander of the country's 1.1 million-strong military, and three vice presidents.
Kim Jong-il has yet to be formally confirmed as state president and general secretary of the ruling Workers' Party -- two key posts left vacant by the death of his father, Kim Il-sung, in 1994.
Many North Korea watchers say Kim Jong-il is likely to formally assume the posts after the third anniversary of his father's death in July.

"North Korea is expected to whip up threats of war to help cement unity and maintain its system," Park said. "Kim Jong-il's reliance on the military will have to continue as long as the North faces a crisis."
Hwang Jang-yop, the most senior North Korean official to flee the communist country, warned on arrival in Seoul last week that Pyongyang was bent on war preparation.
Famine-threatened North Korea remains technically at war with the south because the 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce rather than a peace treaty.
